Second, when the House adjourns today it will stand adjourned until Monday, April 17, 1972, at 2 o'clock p.m., the result being that there will be no sitting of the House tomorrow morning or afternoon. The address of the President is an address to a joint meeting of the House of Commons and the Senate. It is not a sitting of the House in the normal sense. That arrangement will permit the facilities to be prepared for the address tomorrow afternoon.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 EXTERNAL AFFAIRS CANADA-UNITED STATES RELATIONS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, pursuant to Standing Order 26 I ask leave, seconded by the hon. member for Hillsborough, to move the adjournment of the House in order to discuss a specific and important matter requiring urgent consideration, namely the issues which are or ought to be discussed between President Nixon and the Prime Minister on the occasion of the visit of the President of the United States to Ottawa, including, in particular, questions dealing with trade relations, foreign investment, pipeline construction from northern parts of the continent, pollution and the Alaska Highway, so that the members of this House, as the representatives of the people, might be able to indicate the views of the people of Canada.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 EXTERNAL AFFAIRS CANADA-UNITED STATES RELATIONS
speechtext:
I have serious reservations as to the form of the presentation of the hon. member for Peace River and of the notice he has given to the Chair, but I can confirm that the hon. member has in fact given notice of his intention to move the adjournment of the House for

the purpose of discussing a specific and important matter under the provisions of Standing Order 26.
There is little doubt that the subject matter of the hon. member's proposal is of great importance and that the matters he would like the House to consider today are of current and national interest. My difficulty is to determine whether the proposal, though I fully recognize its timeliness, importance and national interest, meets the requirements for immediate debate at this particular moment under the provisions of Standing Order 26.
My understanding of Standing Order 26 is that its provisions relate to a genuine emergency arising suddenly and requiring immediate debate. It does seem to me that the President's projected visit to Ottawa has been common knowledge to members of the House prior to the Easter adjournment. As early as October 15 last it was the subject matter of a question and a reply in the House. The proposed visit was formally announced in the Speech from the Throne on February 17 last. Hon. members need not be reminded that the debate on the address did provide an opportunity to discuss the several topics enumerated by the hon. member for Peace River. Furthermore, each one of these matters has been raised in the House on a number of occasions in the course of debates on supply motions, during the question period, during adjournment proceedings and, as I have said, during the address debate. In light of these circumstances it would be exceedingly difficult for the Chair to allow the motion at this time.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INDUSTRIAL RELATIONS, LABOUR RELATIONS BOARD, INDUSTRIAL INQUIRY COMMISSIONS AND CONCILIATION BOARDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it seems to be particularly pertinent to have today this opportunity to discuss a bill respecting industrial relations in Canada.
All hon. members are currently watching the province of Quebec where a major conflict is paralyzing the public and para-public services. I am quite aware that the Quebec jurisdiction is the only one involved but the citizens cannot be prevented from wondering about the validity of our industrial relations system. This unfortunate event once more emphasizes that labour relations are a major problem in Canadian society and this problem will prevail until new structures are adopted to keep to a minimum the impact of industrial conflicts.
The public discussion of these unfortunate developments is caracterized by two main concepts: first, we have the reactionaries who are advocating the use of the whole legal machinery to impose solutions to these conflicts, starting with compulsory arbitration and up to labour relations lectures.
In this connection, the experience in New Zealand and Australia, where they have compulsory arbitration, proves beyond a doubt that it is not the solution. Industrial conflicts are not solved by making them illegal. When an illegal strike breaks out, the conciliation services of the state are not available. Despite everything, some people maintain that strikes must be declared illegal, that the strikers must be forced back to work, through illegal interventions.
At the other extreme we find those whom I would call adventurers, that is, those who claim that unions do not have enough power, that the state should give them the necessary tools or means to fight for the interests of their members. In practice, those people ask the state to take a stand in favour of union members while, traditionally, the state has played the role of mediator.
Half-way between these two trends of thought, a good many Canadians, while recognizing the positive part played by the trade unions on the one hand, and the dynamism shown by employers on the other hand, admit that public interest should prevail in such conflicts.
At the present time, the province of Quebec is passing through dramatic hours since hospital, school and other public services are almost paralysed. Such a state of affairs, apart from the blame to be assumed by the parties, simply shows that the present system is faulty and that time has come to correct it.
Also, I should like to point to a situation indicating that the present system, if improved through the amendments now before the House, could promote the development of sound relations between employers and employees.
Some ten days ago, the Montreal dockers ratified a contract, signed by their representative, guaranteeing labour peace for three years. Since a large number of the workers affected by this settlement live in my riding, I hastened to get in touch with some of them, in order to obtain further information on this situation; contrary to the first instance I have quoted, it unfortunately did not make headlines in this country's papers.

The history of the port of Montreal is one of trouble, uneasiness and walk-outs, in which mingled violence and organized crime. Since the creation of the specialists system by industry, the Department of Labour has promised to correct the situation and, for the first time in the history of the port of Montreal, a collective agreement has just been signed, without any work stoppage nor compulsory arbitration being imposed on the parties involved.
I wish to insist on that fact because the shipping industry is a pioneer in the field of technological development and serves, as it were, as a laboratory for modern techniques of transportation. Consequently, there is greater insecurity among and lower productivity by the workers concerned, both major causes of labour disputes.
How is it that in such circumstances the parties involved are able to voluntarily sign a contract which will be binding upon them for the next three years? How is it that in the present situation, which is favourable to the development of labour relations problems giving rise to strikes and often to violence, we should see the industry rationalize its relations and conclude this pact which is to the advantage of all parties concerned? This contract is the result of a constant dialogue, an almost stubborn dialogue between the two parties which, every day for the last three years, have met and tried first of all to identify their problems, to explore all possible solutions and to chose the best one. Labour and management at the port of Montreal are used to talking with one another, to confronting one another, to negotiating and to coming to agreements. It is therefore not surprising that in such circumstances they can come to a peaceful solution of their problems.
This collective agreement is clearly geared to job security. That question was recognized as the primary issue at the port of Montreal. In fact, the salary increases are negligible: 2 per cent the first year, 4 per cent the second year and 4 per cent the third year. How was it possible when we see settlements of 10 or even 15 per cent a year? The settlement became possible because the parties concerned did not hesitate to tackle the problems which they faced. On the other hand, the employer has frankly considered the issue of employment security and taken all possible means to find an answer. The union, for its part, has refused to resort to blackmail in connection with the other clauses of the collective agreement which did not give rise to any important problem. Their agreement probably includes the best plan for security of employment in the country and the employer finds it profitable. The agreement eliminates traditional practices to restrict production, increases standardization of working hours, provides a better definition of each job, in short gives a professional status to the longshoremen. This agreement deals with the whole problem of the effects of technological change. These provisions allow the employer to rely on the stability of his personnel for the next three years.
The purpose of the bill now before the House is to extend to all industries under federal jurisdiction the concept of early negotiations concerning problems which recur during all negotiations. Technological change cannot be ignored. It is a condition for the survival of the employer. Failure to mechanize equipment, introduce new
April 13, 1972

machinery and streamline operations makes it impossible for him to compete, not only on international markets, but locally. Nor can the workers ignore technological change. They see it as a threat to their livelihood and are prepared to make any sacrifice to prevent lay-offs which usually follow its introduction. It is suggested that the parties meet around a negotiation table to discuss these matters and arrive at an agreement.
It seems to me that we have there-and the case of the port of Montreal proves it-all the conditions favouring industrial peace. Some employers were reticent about our proposals, alleging that we were giving greater power to the union, the power to control the introduction of technological changes. Some union members claimed that we were not going far enough, that the union should be absolutely free to introduce these changes. I think that the solution suggested here is a happy compromise taking into account the employer's obligation to follow the progress of modern technology and respecting the worker's right to minimum security through collective bargaining.
As for so-called public interest disputes, the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander) has suggested the establishment of a commission which would be asked to investigate in that field. I find it difficult to accept that on so vital a matter as that regarding disputes of public interest the first responsibility be given to a non-elected and independent commission which, to all intents and purposes, has no more power than the minister of labour (Mr. O'Connell). In my opinion, in circumstances such as these, the one who must assume the responsibility for the settlement of these disputes must be a member of the government elected for this purpose. I don't think the Minister of Labour should shun his responsibilities by submitting disputes to a third party.
Mr. Speaker, the bill would also provide the right of bargaining rights for professional employees, owners and drivers of trucks and fishermen; it also aims at reconstituting the Labour Relations Board into a full time organization with increased powers, to reinforce the clauses pertaining to unfair practices in order to further protect employers and the union members; it also provides the Minister of Labour with a greater number of instruments to enable him to settle disputes.
As long as we are willing and co-operate, we will achieve this objective and overcome the difficulties brought about by the automation era.
(English)

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INDUSTRIAL RELATIONS, LABOUR RELATIONS BOARD, INDUSTRIAL INQUIRY COMMISSIONS AND CONCILIATION BOARDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Bill C-183 now before us for second reading is of such importance and far reaching magnitude it is surprising to me to note the haste with which the government has presented it to the House in an attempt to rush it through. After all the months of consideration of the Woods and various other reports on labour-management relations, along with the introduction of the infamous bill C-253 which came to such a dismal end, I should have thought that when the government introduced the revamped and watered down Bill C-183, it would have given the House a greater opportunity to study the changes in order that a reasonable assessment of the worth of these changes may be made.
Canada Labour Code
Bill C-183 was given first reading on March 27 and was brought into the House for second reading on March 29, at which time very few members had ever seen the bill. It was impossible for us on this side to make a reasonable assessment when we had not even seen it. I thought the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander) did an excellent job in presenting his and our views, even though when working largely in the dark because he had only had the bill before him for a very few minutes. I agree with his statement that we on this side feel revisions to the Labour Code are long overdue. We agree with certain changes and with the need for an overhaul of the code, but there are certain clauses in the new bill about which we still have reservations. We will examine them more thoroughly in the committee.
It was encouraging to have the minister give his consent to the suggestion of the hon. member for Hamilton West that those people who have representations to make on this bill be heard. I hope this will be done in the committee as it will give us a much better opportunity to assess all the implications of Bill C-183, and the changes from Bill C-253 which was so abnoxious to so many people. In case I am accused of exaggeration in referring to the fact that the previous bill, on which this bill was modelled, was abnoxious to people, I should like to refer to a letter I received from one of my constituents who happens to be the general manager of one of the largest employers in the area. He said that the bill was so one sided it gave one the impression of having been drafted by a labour fanatic.
The Labour Code needs to be amended, certainly, but where are the amendments we as Canadians, not just employers and employees, really need? What about legislation dealing with public interest contracts and making the unions legal entities? How long do we have to put up with the use of power by unions because of the present imbalance of power? When are we going to differentiate between a wildcat strike and a long study session, and when are unions going to be responsible for personal property damage caused by so-called lack of administrative control?
While I hasten to inform the House that this letter refers to Bill C-253 and not the bill presently before us, it is a good indication of the feelings of a great body of Canadians today. The Canadian public is worried about the obvious breakdown in relations between management and labour. When the member who spoke earlier began his remarks, he referred to the unhappy situation in Quebec and indicated that this whole matter is one of urgent and pressing concern to all Canadians. It is time the government took some action to resolve this conflict between labour and management.
At the time Bill C-253 was introduced, it was interesting to read a comment by Mr. David Peach, assistant professor of the school of business administration at Western University. The article by Mr. Peach, which appeared in the Financial Post, reads in part:
The government, in my opinion, has introduced a piece of absurd legislation, and its implications should be of real concern to managers everywhere, even though the immediate application of the legislation is limited to the federal jurisdiction.
He goes on to refer to the provisions in the first bill which would allow collective agreements to be reopened

during the life of a contract. I realize that this has been altered in the present bill. The article continues:
Presumably, the government wants to encourage the development of contract provisions which would provide workers with protection against the effects of technological change. The proposed legislation will not achieve this aim. If the government is serious in its intent, it appears the legislation will have to be changed.
A strong case can be made for eliminating the proposed provisions on technological change altogether.
Without agreeing or disagreeing with Professor Peach, I quoted from his article in order to illustrate the great concern Canadians generally have about this type of labour legislation. Is this the best way to create harmony between management and labour? Surely, this is the key to the whole problem. Without that harmony we can legislate from now until kingdom come and nothing will be accomplished. We must have that harmony between management and labour. We should be trying to decide the best way to develop that harmony.
Professor Peach went on to refer to the earlier bill. He said this was the wrong way to develop harmony, that it would only create further antagonism and lead to more strikes and lockouts. He went on to say:
However, there is a better way of going about this than what Mackasey proposes. The solution lies in the 1968 Woods task force report on labor relations.
These few remarks are intended as a background to the concern I wish to express on behalf of myself and those on this side of the House about the chaotic state of labour-management relations today. It is not my intention to point the finger at or place the blame on anyone. However, in discussing this bill I should like to make perhaps four or five specific suggestions concerning areas of the bill which I believe are undesirable and should be changed.
I shall refer to some of the things the bill does not do. While I agree with my colleague from Hamilton West that changes in the labour code are desirable, I wish to enter a caveat that we will consider each of the clauses in the bill in committee and reserve the right to suggest amendments as we see fit. What are the things the bill purports to do or does not do? To start with, the bill, admittedly, represents a considerable improvement over Bill C-253. The technological change clause has been watered down, but here again we will not know the effect of it until we have had an opportunity to study the clause in depth after hearing representations from representatives of management and labour. The wording of the clause is obscure. The minister's opening statement left a bit of doubt concerning how far this change would go. The point is not clear and, therefore, should be discussed extensively in the committee.
The bill is unimaginative and weak in respect of reducing the incidence of strikes and lockouts and their effect on the public interest. I cannot see any provision in this bill that would in any way alleviate the chaotic conditions which exist today. I suggest that some of the provisions in the bill possibly could aggravate present conditions. Those who drafted the bill failed to take advantage of many of the suggestions contained in the Woods report of

1968. I will refer to one or two of these later. The hon. member who spoke previously mentioned that we advocated, or that the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander) advocated, a suggestion contained in the Woods report which he felt was an excellent suggestion.
As I read it, Bill C-183 affects some 530,000 employees in the public service which covers people in the fields of transportation, pipelines, communications and many other federal services. The bill, however, does not affect collective bargaining in respect of public servants who are members of NABET and employees of the CBC, or those who are covered by the Public Service Staff Relations Act. I know members opposite and the minister might say the bill is not intended to do this because those employees are covered by a separate piece of legislation. I agree. However, it seems to me that one of the greatest concerns of Canadians today, whether or not they are hockey fans, is the continuing frustration caused by the fact that a few members of a relatively small union are able in effect to throw the whole country into disruption, anger and disgust. It seems to me this is one of the aspects we should be looking at in respect of this bill or in respect of some clauses which might be added to it.
Another subject which interests members on this side- and this was referred to by the hon. member for Hamilton West-is the Canada Labour Relations Board. The bill will set up this board much along the lines suggested by the Woods report with a chairman, a vice-chairman and four to eight members who would be appointed full time by the Governor in Council. What disturbs us is the fact that the method by which members of the board would be appointed would do nothing to make the board representative of management and labour. We feel there should be an amendment which would ensure an advisory role for management and labour in respect of the appointment of some of the members of the board. This is one suggestion we would have for the improvement of the bill.
The bill also extends bargaining rights. Many more employees will be brought under the umbrella of collective bargaining. The bill would extend bargaining rights to certain professional and supervisory people. Here again, however, the wording of the bill is fuzzy. It is unclear just who would be included under this particular provision. At a time when there is such a great deal of dispute between management and labour, there is also the question of whether it is wise to extend these rights.
I might refer to a brief presented by Domtar Limited in respect of Bill C-253, in which the following point is made:
The extension of collective bargaining rights to professional and supervisory groups at a time when collective bargaining appears to be creating serious economic and social problems is questionable. Existing problems, including the impact on inflation, should be better understood before collective bargaining is extended to new areas. It is suggested that the confines of collective bargaining be kept within the present boundaries until we have learned how to cope with existing problems.
Again, by extending collective bargaining to professional groups, we could very well be faced with a closed shop for professional people.
The Woods Report, at page 149, reads:
. . . that, in a unit for which a union is the bargaining agent, a member must pay the regular and reasonable
April 13, 1972

dues of the union whether he takes out a membership or not, as an "agency fee".
This is widely known as an agency shop, and is recognized in the bill. However, the bill goes beyond this to provide legal acceptance of the closed shop, which has been regarded as increasingly indefensible by the Woods Report and has been criticized by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). Section 161 expressly states that the collective agreements may contain a clause requiring, as a condition of employment, membership in a specified trade union or preference in employment may be given to members of a specified trade union. This section, along with section 125(3), creates the possibility of the very kind of closed shop the Prime Minister has been urging provinces to move against. Taken together, these provisions allow professional employees, doctors, lawyers, engineers, scientists, accountants and so on to establish separate bargaining units and to exclude from employment other professionals who are not members of their union. The government is inviting the kinds of uneconomic and unjust employment restrictions that are far too prevalent at the provincial level at this time. The taxpayers ~nd university graduates need fewer, not more, impediments to employment. I think we should discuss these clauses very carefully in committee and possibly suggest some changes.
I think this bill does not go far enough in another area which I mentioned earlier. In fact you could say that, as written, the bill does very little to promote industrial peace. All of us are concerned about this today. Strikes and lockouts are on the increase. On this side of the House, we feel that it is time the government took remedial action to correct the situation.
Allied with industrial peace is the whole problem of the effect of strikes on the public interest. This aspect has been discussed many times, and the Woods report arrived at some fairly realistic conclusions about it. However, unless and until the government is prepared to offer a solution on how to handle strikes which affect the public interest, the chaos which exists today will continue. Many of the provisions in the bill will serve the public interest by providing machinery to reduce the likelihood of strikes and lockouts, but the bill fails to protect the public in the event of strikes and lockouts in essential services.
One proposal of the Woods task force which was referred to earlier today, and was endorsed in principle by the Progressive Conservative party last year, is as follows:
A Public Interest Disputes Commission should be established to determine special procedures for resolving industrial disputes for essential services. If the commission is unsuccessful in its efforts it should report to parliament on the situation which would thereby have a more comprehensive and informed basis on which to exercise the power it now has to legislate an end to a strike or lockout.
The question of a public interest disputes commission has been discussed many times. 1 think it is a logical solution, a sort of court of appeal in labour relations. Certainly, it is worth a trial and possibly such a provision should be included in this legislation. It is not a departure from the principle of free collective bargaining which
Canada Labour Code
should remain the cornerstone of industrial relations in Canada. Machinery is provided for finding new ways for collective bargaining compatible with the public interest, as well as assisting parliament in rationally and competently exercising the authority it now has to protect the public interest.
I believe the clauses in the original bill, C-253, which caused the greatest concern and the greatest protest, were those which dealt with technological change. This is a difficult subject. How does one arrive at a tidy balance between the necessity for industry to be competitive by improving its methods, while at the same time ensuring that not too many people suffer loss and deprivation as a result of change? I know the minister is well aware of this, and I was interested to hear him refer to it in his opening statement. He pointed out the necessity for Canadian industry to compete successfully with foreign industry by keeping up with the times, but on the other hand he realises that the result of such changes on workers must be minimized by realistic legislation.
In all this talk of technological change, whenever a company modernizes machinery or introduces new production equipment, we hear the cry that it is all very fine but it is going to throw people out of work. It is the old cry which was heard back in the days of the industrial revolution, the machine would lead to great production but everybody would be out of work. Anyone who has studied economic history would question the veracity of the statement that technological change is necessarily bad. I was interested in a submission by the Canadian Chamber of Commerce in which it is stated:
Contrary to fears expressed by some people some years ago that technological changes would result in a substantial net reduction in the number of jobs, the fact is that advancing technology has created more new jobs than have been rendered redundant because of it. Thus, any impediment to technological change helps restrict new employment opportunities.
I do not accept that statement 100 per cent because it is a grey area. Figures can be produced on either side but, on balance, it would be very difficult to show that technological change has been bad for all industrial nations. I think it would be much easier to show that without technological change the great nations of the world would not have advanced to the position they are in today. Let us not get caught up in emotion and say that technological changes are necessarily bad and must be controlled, otherwise people will be thrown out of work. I suggest to the House that it is not as simple as that. Technological change is not necessarily bad and we should be very careful not to introduce legislation which might discourage companies from making such changes as are necessary if they are to compete in the world today.
The importance of this must be evident to this House in view of the fact that for the past year and a half we have had agitated debate on the difficulties faced by Canada when competing in world markets. We recall what happened last August when the United States took retaliatory measures to correct their adverse balance of trade. We know what is happening in the markets of Japan and Germany, as well as in the rest of the world, with the economic conditions that exist today. In view of the state of world currency, it becomes more and more important for Canadian industry to keep abreast of scientific,

April 13, 1972
Canada Labour Code
modern production methods so that we can sell our goods at a competitive price. The question of gearing up production has become more important in the past few years because of several trends. The rise in value of the Canadian dollar has increased foreign competition and required Canadian industry to search for more efficient and recognized means of production.
On the other hand a high level of unemployment, government initiated and therefore out of control, prevents the re-absorption of displaced semi-skilled and unskilled occupational groups into the Canadian labour force. Where Canadian industries have failed to take advantage of technological advances, as in the pulp and paper industry, labour lay-offs have resulted. Many of the problems we are now experiencing in New Brunswick, with lay-offs in the pulp and paper mills, are largely due to the fact that mills did not keep pace with modern production methods. As a result, they find themselves unable to compete with modern plants which use improved methods of production.
Obviously labour and management are directly concerned and interested in technological change. But it is equally obvious, although not generally recognized and admitted, that the Canadian public has an interest. There are reasons for this. In the first place, the Canadian public has an interest as the beneficiary of an efficient and technologically competitive industry, or as the financial victim of an inefficient industry that is protected by tariffs or bolstered by subsidies. In the second place, the Canadian public is interested as the tax source whose taxes are used to assist industry to make technological changes or to assist employees to weather such changes. In the third place, the Canadian public is interested as the victim inconvenienced by industrial strife arising out of the failure of management and labour to reach agreement on technological change.
This public interest is not one of convenience or inconvenience but of responsibility, for the public is responsible for the economic, fiscal, tax, tariff and trade policies of the government of the day. These policies may encourage or discourage an industry in making technological change, or encourage or discourage labour from cooperating in such change. It is reasonable to conclude that the public has a vested interest in the problems of technological change and, arising out of that interest, a right and a responsibility to be a third presence with management and trade unions in contributing to the solution of such problems.
If I have dwelt over long on that particular aspect of the bill, Mr. Speaker, I have done so deliberately because that is something which needs repeating. Since Bill C-253 was introduced, it seems that all we have heard has been the views of the two opposing sides, one saying that technological changes will put workers out of jobs, and the other upholding management by saying that technological changes must be made in order for industry to stay alive in the business world. The present minister has made an attempt to water down the technological change provisions in this bill in order to make it acceptable to both management and labour. His predecessor absolutely refused to do this. But we on this side do not know if the

changes made in this bill are exactly what they seem to be on the surface. How far do they go? This is what we must discuss in committee. With all due respect, Mr. Speaker, the wording is fuzzy and vague. Perhaps we have not had time to sit down and read these provisions closely ten or 12 times, although I doubt that repetitious reading would make the words any clearer.
I question if the bill has been modified to the extent that the newspapers would have us believe. However, I want to approach the matter with an open mind. If the minister can convince me of this in committee then I will say, "More power to you; we are all for it." But it is important that we not be stampeded by one side or the other, by business into saying these changes are bad or by labour into saying these changes must be made. It is time somebody started thinking of the Canadian public caught between the two groups.
Just before sitting down, I would like to refer to another aspect of the bill which disturbs me. I suppose hon. members on the other side of the House become tired hearing me talk about this matter time and time again. When the unemployment insurance bill was before the House I said over and over again that it was too complicated and would be impossible to administer. I said the wording of the clauses was fuzzy and too much was left to be filled in by ministerial regulations. The minister and his officials pooh-poohed my contention. They said anybody could understand the bill. We all know what the result has been. I am afraid that this bill will leave itself open to another administrative mess as bad as or worse than anything we have seen under the Unemployment Insurance Act. Here again, I refer to Professor Peach's remarks in reference to Bill C-253, but which are still valid so far as this bill is concerned because there is no basic change with respect to the administration of this measure. Professor Peach said:
I have not yet mentioned the administrative difficulties the act presents. What criteria are the government, the Labour Board, or the parties going to use to define just what constitutes a technological change? What is meant by a "significant" number of employees?
The minister or the Governor in Council can decide this.
In short, the act is an administrative nightmare.
The proposed revisions constitute a piece of mischievious legislation, one that can logically cast the government as a latter day Luddite. And to what end? Is the legislation really needed?
In the aggregate, technological change does not hurt anyone. The substitution of machine power for man power has been a constant factor in man's development. Despite the increasing rate at which change is occurring and despite a number of gloomy prophesies, a full-employment economy can be a reality today.
Ideally, the government, I think, should limit itself to providing the proper fiscal and monetary policies that will maintain a level of aggregate demand sufficient to provide full employment.
The government is unlikely to restrict its role in this manner, but if activism is to be the rule of the day, a better alternative exists in the Woods Report recommendations.
Hopefully, the government will change its mind in regard to this legislation. If not, we can be thankful that the federal jurisdiction is not the only one in Canadian labour relations.
Business should be aware of the traps that exist in legislation of this kind, and work to keep provincial law free from contamination by this kind of fuzzy thinking.
The professor may have been a little harsh and too critical. I am willing to be convinced. I hope the minister
April 13, 1972

will be able to convince me and my colleagues in the committee that he has made significant changes in this bill. I also hope that some of the other matters I have raised today will be discussed in the committee. If the changes made in this bill prove to be undesirable, I hope that the minister will accept amendments, if not from this side of the House at least from his own side. We accept the fact that the Labour Code needs revision. We are quite prepared to let this bill go to committee where we will examine it carefully. We have reservations with respect to certain clauses, and we hope that in committee the minister will give a frank and full appraisal of how the bill is an improvement over Bill C-253.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in speaking on this bill to amend the Canada Labour Code I will at this stage try to keep my remarks general, and related to the principles of the bill and of labour-management relations.
As I look at labour-management problems in this country, and in many others, I wonder if we are progressing very much by introducing legislative measures such as the one now before us, measures which are designed to solve one or several very particular problems, but in many instances are only adding to the irritants which, to my mind, create the great difficulty in labour negotiations. These irritants seem to be endless in number and make adversaries of the parties involved. It is not really the basic principles which cause the serious controversies between labour and management but, rather, the small items which become so important by virtue of their numbers.
Relations between labour and management are like those between a husband and wife who cannot get along, Mr. Speaker, not because they disagree on their basic responsibilities in marriage, family and such, but because of the constant small peckings of one or the other and the wall that the great number of these minor peckings builds between them. I wonder if measures such as the one we are debating do not add to the irritation and do not just build that wall higher and higher between the two parties. How unfortunate it would be if that were so. Every time we add another law, Mr. Speaker, another regulation and another clause in this area, we restrict the basic principle that the preamble proclaims in this bill, the principle of collective bargaining.
I have to chuckle a little every time I see that phrase, "collective bargaining", which, in theory, represents an ideal vehicle for resolving mutual problems between parties. As the theory is put into practice, it would be more appropriate to refer to it as "collective pressure bargaining", since the major, meaningful factor in these negotiations is simply the pressure that one party can bring to bear upon the other, most often not to obtain a proper and equitable agreement but to obtain for that party whatever that pressure can get. Imagine, Mr. Speaker, a system for solving the problems of two parties under which each party tries to hurt the other party to gain its own advantage, whereas the theory of the system implies mutual participation and co-operation.
I continue to be amazed that, with all the wisdom we have, the technological advances we have made, the
Canada Labour Code
advances in the social sciences that have taken place, and so on, we have not yet developed methods for solving problems that are superior to the strikes that are harmful to all, including the always innocent third party, the public. I think it is pure fantasy to say we believe in the collective bargaining process and then place all sorts of restrictions on that process, such as the clauses included in this legislative measure. If we are sincere in saying collective bargaining works, then we should let it work freely, as the principle implies, rather than impose all sorts of restrictions. If we need these restrictions, I think we should have the courage to admit that the system does not work as we feel it should, and governments should have the courage to look at something else.
It is said that the clauses in the bill before us regarding technological changes incorporate a new and important principle. Mr. Speaker, I do not think it is a new principle. It may be a concept; certainly, it is not a principle. If it were a principle, it would have the same basic importance for all and would have equal meaning to all parties concerned. I submit that it will have no such balance in meaning and justice. The concept is simply another restriction placed on the true principle of collective bargaining. It is another concept that will become, in numerous cases, one further irritant. It will not apply to all parties alike. It will mean different things in different situations and will have different results in different cases. I like to think principles are more universal and more basic than that, and if the government feels compelled to bring in such concepts, why does it not develop measures and standards that will apply to all workers and not just to the organized people who have the power to negotiate their own agreements? I hardly think it akin to good federalism for a federal government to be enacting measures that discriminate between organized and nonorganized labour.

There is no justifiable criterion for that sort of distinction, especially by a national government. If the preamble to this bill means that we are entrenching a principle in law that does not now work well and if we are saying that its effectiveness is unquestionable, then I am opposed to that preamble; for, obviously, the principle it enunciates is not the be all and end all in this area. If it were, why would we be bending and altering it by such restrictions as we find in this piece of legislation? Why must we so often be looking at legislation which-is presented simply to solve specific short term problems and to render administration more efficient and easy, instead of recognizing and applying the principles and policies of right and justice.
If the government, Mr. Speaker, feels it is necessary to initiate measures such as those in this bill, I say there is a long list of practical measures that could be implemented to eliminate the dreadful irritants of labour-management relations. They are not included in this bill and they, I feel, would be more helpful. Why not identify clearly and describe the responsibilities and privileges that are imposed or granted to both parties involved in strikes and lockouts, so that those responsibilities and privileges clearly mean one thing to everybody and not ten different things to ten different people? Why not establish a clear

April 13, 1972
Canada Labour Code
distinction between the private sector, which can use an economic factor as a measure of pressure, and the public sector, which can use no such measure. The public sector is sometimes thought to have available to it a bottomless pit, from which both parties to the negotiation can obtain, or give out, unlimited benefits. Surely, there is a good case to be made for having two different governing principles for these two completely different sectors. Why not include the national interest and the interest of innocent third parties as a recognized and valid factor in all such matters.
When we see the present situation in Quebec caused by the common front of public service employees who are openly recommending an illegal disregard of court injunctions applying to those employees, who are flouting and confronting the legal governmental authority, and therefore the citizens themselves-in all probability for political reasons-we realize, surely, that the bounds of responsibility towards the public are being cast aside for the benefit only of a certain group. Why not do something about preventing the dropping of legal charges as part of a settlement, once these charges, which might involve civil or criminal proceedings, have been laid for acts of violence, illegal strikes or lockouts, or fraud and all other such reasons. Surely, permitting such practices ridicules the laws of the country and encourages the continuation and propagation of such illegal acts.
Why not look at the practical, discriminatory situation which allows organized employers to refuse employment to a non-union member but prevents a non-organized employer from requesting non-union employees from Canada Manpower Centres. Is it not time finally to consider making labour organizations legal entities, with full capacity to sue and be sued? Surely, any labour body which is sincere and honest would not object to accepting its full responsibility in our society. Surely, there is no need to excuse these organizations from legal responsibility in order for them to fulfil properly their function in society. Why not review the ridiculous situation caused by illegal strikes, lockouts or slowdowns that now have become normal practice and for which there seems to be no effective remedy? Surely, there is no justification for such practices and our laws and labour boards should not condpne, but condemn these actions very severely. All of these, Mr. Speaker, and there are many more, are irritants in the labour-management process. All of these prevent the co-operation and mutual respect between management and labour that is essential for the smooth, effective relations that are necessary for the development of industry and the recognition of human values which all contribute to the prosperity of this country.
I certainly hope, Mr. Speaker, that the measures in this bill have not been introduced simply as a sop to Mr. MacDonald and his Canadian Labour Congress, since I cannot think of any person or organization whose presentations or opinions would be more biased or tainted with the political clap-trap of the NDP which that organization finances, for which they labour and whose political interests they always promote and reflect in any of their representations.

A few of the representations were very shortsighted; however, most of them included some very worth-while comments and recommendations. I am convinced that the minister now responsible for this bill has given full consideration to these representations. I have enough confidence in his objectivity to feel that he will give further consideration to all further recommendations. I also know that the minister will not judge suggestions made by their source but, rather, their merit.
Some observations made about governmental affairs are sometimes very surprising, and especially so when one considers the authors of those observations. For instance, when Mr. McLaughlin, as president of a large Canadian chartered bank says his bank will continue to finance American take-overs of Canadian companies because if it does not some other bank will, he demonstrates a restricted concern for Canadian society and enterprise that is close to being unbelievable. Of course, somebody else will finance such take-overs. I doubt very much if Mr. McLaughlin's bank would finance such deals if they were not sound enough to be attractive to someone else. Canadian bankers are well noted for their conservatism in lending, but surely the point is not who would finance such deals but whether that bank should not be using its funds to provide Canadian industry with the money it needs. Surely, a Canadian Chartered bank has a national and social responsibility which Mr. McLaughlin completely ignores here. Surely, industry, commerce and finance are elements of society and their function is to serve that society, not the other way around. The leaders of industry and commerce have a social responsibility which they cannot ignore, and ignoring it begs governments to step in and impose measures that satisfy that responsibility.
The free enterprise system itself will not endure if the private sector refuses its social responsibilty. Every time a
April 13, 1972

government must initiate another program or regulation to serve the needs of our citizens, a further erosion occurs. We regularly hear the opposition parties and uninformed individuals attribute total responsibility for unemployment, the creating of jobs, the expansion of the economy to the government, but in a free enterprise system it is industry and commerce which create jobs, expand production, and find markets. If industry, with the assistance it can reasonably and rightfully expect from government, does not look after the unemployed, the invalids, the needy, then it should not chastise the government for doing so, thereby fulfilling the responsibility that a society has toward its individual members. Governments set out the goals and aspirations that remain targets for the nation, but flowing from those goals there should be a periodic, clear indentification of the areas of responsibility for government, industry, labour or the general public. Once these are established, all sectors should accept their share of the responsibility for the common good.
Indeed, not only should these responsibilities be accepted, but understood and agreed upon. Such understanding and agreement can only come from meaningful consultation and participation by all, as opposed to tokenism. Sometimes, Mr. Speaker, we ask for representations, discussions and participation, but pay little heed to the observations and recommendations received. Full, sincere consideration must be given to the observations and recommendations presented. It is unworthy to ask for recommendations, receive them, then go around chastising the authors of those recommendations for having expressed their point of view, especially if it differs from our own. In this respect, I have confidence the minister will accept valid and beneficial amendments to the bill at the proper time.

Mr. Speaker, in my ten years in this House, I doubt whether I have ever heard such an anti-labour, anti-union and anti-worker speech as that just made by the hon. member for Timmins (Mr. Roy). Knowing that constituency, knowing how many workers in that area are organized into unions which they have freely and voluntarily chosen and how they will react to the kind of clap-trap which the hon. member for Timmins has just spouted, I can only assume that the hon. member has no intention of running in the next election. I offer my condolences to the Minister of Labour (Mr. O'Connell) because with friends like the hon. member for Timmins, he does not need enemies.
I do not suppose there could be a worse time to discuss a bill dealing with labour-management relations than today. Over 200 thousand people are on strike in the province of Quebec. Civic employees in both Toronto and Vancouver are also on strike. I point out to the hon. member for Timmins that in the province of Quebec, the party which I represent, the New Democratic Party, does not have much support. The hon. member cannot blame us for that strike. I also point out to the hon. member that the Canadian Labour Congress and its affiliated unions are not the main organizations leading the strike in the province of Quebec. The majority of the workers on strike in the province of Quebec are affiliated with unions organized by the Federation of National Trade Unions.
Canada Labour Code
This labour federation was for many years led by the present Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Marchand).
The hon. member for Timmins and all other members should be worried about the strikes in the province of Quebec, Vancouver and Toronto. We should all be asking why these strikes are taking place. For almost 100 years labour unions were comprised almost exclusively of blue collar workers, workers in the manufacturing and transportation fields. Of the strikes which took place, 99 per cent were in industry and transportation, the blue collar field. Why do we suddenly have strikes by groups of workers who were not even organized 10 years ago? Until recently these groups refused to admit they belonged to unions, although they sometimes had large organizations which they called associations. We now have strikes of teachers, hospital employees, baseball players and transportation technicians. Why do we have these strikes?
An hon. member from the official opposition spoke earlier today. He compared the difficulties in Canada with the relative peace in terms of labour-management relations in such countries as Japan. For years we have been told that we ought to look at Sweden. Why are there not many strikes in countries like Japan and Sweden? I am sure the Minister of Labour knows for a fact that one of the reasons they do not have strikes is that they have had almost continuously, at least since the end of World War II, virtually full employment. If a company develops a new process, technology or system of operation and a worker or group of workers will be laid-off, the worker knows that the economy of the country is working in such a way that he will get another job. That worker is not likely to be too concerned. He is not likely to go on strike or to demand guarantees that his particular job will be protected, because he knows the economy is working in such a way as to allow him to get a new job if he is laid-off an old one.
The situation in Canada is unfortunately entirely different. For a dozen years or more we have witnessed large-scale unemployment. Under the present government the number of unemployed has doubled in the last four years as compared with the last four years of the Pearson Liberal administration. For almost two years, with the exception of last month, unemployment has been running at the rate of 6 per cent or more on a seasonally-adjusted basis. As hon. members know, NABET members are in dispute with the CBC. Let me make it clear that I am not at the moment saying they are justified in making all the demands they are putting forward. But these workers know there have been major changes in technology, that a great deal of automation has taken place in the field of television, and that a great deal more will take place in the near future. When they see this happening, and realize that hundreds if not thousands of jobs in their industry will disappear, they say: we do not want to bear the entire brunt of this change; we want some protection, certain guarantees. I cannot blame them for doing so, and I do not think the Minister of Labour will blame them either, particularly since the company, in this case the CBC, has virtually refused to discuss the question. In these circumstances, one cannot blame workers for being upset.
1304

April 13, 1972
Canada Labour Code
Significant changes are taking place in the field of education. I realize that education is not a federal responsibility, but the illustration I propose to use will make it clear why people are concerned about the basic principle in the bill before us. Year after year, for many years, more and more people have been attending schools. As a result, cities and provinces were hiring more and more teachers. Today, for various reasons, the trend is reversed. I am told, for example, that in my own City of Winnipeg there has been a reduction of 2,000 in the student population in the last two years. And this is just a beginning. Teachers will be unemployed. No labour organization I know of has suggested that any person should have the right to keep a job for the rest of his or her life. But people naturally want an assurance, especially if they have worked in an industry or service for a number of years, that they will receive some measure of protection-that the effects of unemployment will be cushioned by early retirements or by keeping people on until sufficient retirements have taken place to ensure that staff reductions are minimized. This is what concerns the workers. This is one of the main causes of the labour unrest we are experiencing now and which we are likely to experience in the future.
The bill we are discussing today looks good. I want to say that the minister made a very sound presentation in introducing it. However, we, together with a great number of ordinary working people, are concerned about the fact that the measure introduced by the minister's predecessor met with such a hostile response from business interests that changes were accepted and embodied in the legislation we have before us. There is a great deal of concern lest these changes may in fact result in weakening the provisions of the legislation, in particular those which have to do with protecting the rights of workers who are adversely affected by technological innovation. Let me put on record just what the minister had to say when he was referring to what had happened since the bill was introduced last year by his predecessor:
In the intervening eight months my predecessor and I, and senior departmental officials, have received representations from-and consulted with-most groups in the country representing management and labour.
Well, I do not think the minister received many representations of an adverse nature from labour organizations. He certainly received a host of very strong representations from management. I want to tell him that, though we approve the bill as it appears on the face of things, and though we like the speech he made, those of our members who will sit on the committee entrusted with examining the measure clause by clause will tend to take a very careful look at the detailed provisions in order to make sure that the ostensible aim as outlined by the minister will in fact be reflected in the legislation. The minister made some comments which seemed to imply important reservations. He said, and I quote again from his speech:
The technological change provisions have been clarified and establish clearly that the collective agreement cannot be re-opened where the employer gives notice of the intended technological change before the agreement was entered into, where the agreement establishes procedures by which the effects of the change may be negotiated and settled, or where there are substantive provisions contained in the agreement that the parties specify are intended to assist the employees affected by the change. Under

these circumstances the collective agreement cannot be re-opened. The technological change provisions would not apply to existing collective agreements but only to those made after the bill comes into force.
Mr. Speaker, how many tens of thousands of workers may be faced by the consequences of important technological changes introduced by their companies before this bill comes into effect? Experience in negotiations between labour and management, and more particularly in arbitration and in court cases, clearly shows that many judges and many arbitrators still cling to what I consider to be an out-dated belief that what is not written into an agreement is the sole prerogative of management to decide, because of the inherent management rights of employers. The concern I have expressed up to now arises from what I consider to be a glaring gap between what this bill provides-what the minister said it provided for in his introductory remarks-and what a man who cannot be called partisan or political by anyone in this House or elsewhere said when he made what I believe to be the most serious, the most honest and the most far-reaching study of this whole question of technological change. I refer to the report made by Mr. Justice Samuel Freedman in 1964 entitled The Report of an Industrial Inquiry Commission on Canadian National Railway Run-Throughs.
For the benefit of members who were not here at the time or who have forgotten let me briefly recapitulate what happened. The CNR announced unilaterally that, effective as of a certain date, certain runs of their freight trains would be virtually doubled in length. In view of the very adverse effect that this change of policy would have, there was a work stoppage. It was unauthorized. I suppose the hon. member for Timmins (Mr. Roy) would say- probably one of the few times he would say something that is correct-that it was an illegal stoppage. But the *ailway workers knew what they were doing. They knew hat probably such as stoppage was a breach of their xisting contract and that it was illegal; but so seized were they of the importance of stopping the company from taking such unilateral action that they were prepared to carry through this illegal stoppage.
In order to get the workers back to work and to get the railways running again, the government of the day proposed the setting up of a one man commission, chaired by Mr. Justice Freedman, to look into the whole question and to make recommendations. On the basis of this proposal by the government, the railway workers went back to work. Mr. Justice Freedman held a number of hearings and looked into the whole question of technological change and its effect upon the work force. He studied the subject in great detail and made a report which I think is a landmark in the history of Canadian labour-management relations. I wish that members of the official opposition, when looking at the record of studies that have been made, would look more to Mr. Justice Freedman's report than to the report made by the Wood commission.
I should like to take a few moments to quote from the section of his report entitled "Technological Change: An Economic and Human Problem". I want to put on the record what Mr. Justice Freedman had to say about the crux of the situation as it affects both management and
April 13, 1972

labour, and the proposals he made which I think are imaginative, far seeing and practical. I hope that when the committee meets to discuss the provisions of this bill, the Minister of Labour and his officials will convince my colleagues on the committee that I am wrong and that the bill really will do the things that Mr. Justice Freedman proposed should be done. We are dealing with perhaps the most fundamental issue dividing workers and management today, an issue that will become more important in the years to come as a result of the tremendous pace at which technological changes are taking place.
If I may just put on the record a few paragraphs from the report by Mr. Justice Freedman, page 132 reads, in part:
Taking a broad, national, long-range view and looking at employment in its totality the economists may be justified in contending that technology does not cause unemployment.
May I digress for a moment to say that this was the argument put forward by one member of the Conservative opposition who spoke earlier this afternoon. It is true that technology and industrialization have meant more production and more work. But this is little comfort for the worker who is displaced, who loses his job because of technological change. It may be that one month, or six months, or even a year or two from the time he is laid off he will have another job, perhaps a better one; but in the interval his situation is pretty grim.
Returning to what Mr. Justice Freedman was saying: Within the total picture, however, technology may bring about individual cases of difficulty and hardship, cases which will be multiplied if the general demand for labour is slack.
Mr. Justice Freedman went on to say this:
But what happens when a technological change releases a factor of production called labour? Clearly it poses problems not so easily written off or disposed of. The old concept of labour as a commodity simply will not suffice; it is at once wrong and dangerous. Hence there is a responsibility upon the entrepreneur who introduces technological change to see that it is not effected at the expense of his working force. That is the human aspect of the technological challenge, and it must not be ignored.
To digress for a moment, that is precisely what labour unions have been saying, no more, no less. I do not know of a single labour organization that has opposed technological change per se. What the labour organizations have said and are saying is that workers affected must not carry the entire brunt or even the major brunt of technological change all by themselves. Then, Mr. Justice Freedman continues:
There are responsibilities upon labour as well. Perhaps chief among them is not to use its organized strength in blind and wilful resistance to technological advances. Labour must recognize the constructive role of technology in the general welfare and economic strength of the nation. Nor should it insist upon unreasonably high rewards or excessive safeguards as the price of its acceptance of change. Stubborn opposition to measures of progress can only hurt the nation, labour not least of all.
If I may again digress, there is probably not an industry in Canada that has, since the end of World War II, seen such a sharp reduction in the total labour force as the railway industry. Not so many years ago the railway unions were negotiating for something in the neighbourhood of 125,000 workers. Today they probably negotiate on behalf of less than 80,000 workers. In other words, there has been a reduction of more than one-third in the
Canada Labour Code
railway labour force at a time when the railways are moving more tons of goods over more miles than ever before. So, no one can say that the railway unions have held out against technological change. What the railway unions are saying is that the ordinary worker must have a modicum of protection.
Then, Mr. Justice Freedman went on to ask whether the CNR had the right to institute the run-throughs which caused the stoppage, and he concluded that they probably did, both on the basis of residual rights and on the basis of the contract as it existed at the time. Then, he went on to say, and I think this is the question at the heart of the legislation we are dealing with today:
Should it-
That is the CNR.
-continue to have that right? The question here raised lies at the heart of this Inquiry. The Commission is satisfied that it must be answered only in one way. The institution of run-throughs should be a matter for negotiation. To treat it as an unfettered management prerogative will only promote unrest, undermine morale, and drive the parties farther and farther apart. In that direction lies disorder and danger.
What was Mr. Justice Freedman's recommendation in this respect? It was a very simple one. It was that where there are major changes in the work force or in working conditions brought on as a result of technological changes, the workers and their unions should have the right to bargain collectively on those changes and have the right to strike, if that is necessary. There is no member of this House who would deny the fact that a strike of railway workers, or of postal workers, or of airline employees, causes difficulties and inconvenience for the whole population. But as Mr. Justice Freedman said so well in his report, surely the workers have the right to protect their own interests, to protect their jobs. In many cases, protecting their jobs means protecting their homes and the communities in which they have lived practically all their lives. That is the crucial issue which supposedly is dealt with in this bill. Mr. Justice Freedman's recommendation was crystal clear; that workers should have the right to bargain collectively when their jobs are seriously affected by changes as a result of technological change and automation brought in by management.
I am sure the minister will agree that this proposal of Mr. Justice Freedman, as well as the one made last year by the former minister when introducing this bill, which would have to some extent implemented the proposals of Mr. Justice Freedman, were met with horror by most employers. They looked at this as another infringement of their God-given right to manage their businesses and plants as they always had, making the major decisions themselves. One cannot blame them for this. As long as this country has existed they have had the right to make major changes without interference from workers, without interference or real question by unions and certainly without interference by government. The employers were horrified and they made their objections clear to the government and, I am sure, to every member of parliament. I do not question their right to their point of view. I should have been amazed had they not taken that view. When this right or privilege has been held as long as the employers
1306

April 13, 1972
Canada Labour Code
have held this privilege of managing their enterprises without question, they begin to regard it as a natural right. If it appears that there is to be interference, it is no wonder we hear a tremendous outcry from the business community.
I hope the provisions of the bill as drafted and presented by the minister will not prove to be a capitulation, even in part, to what I consider to be unwarranted fears on the part of the employers of this country. I hope this bill will do those things it seems to do, and which the minister indicated it would do when he introduced it. I hope when the bill is passed, as I am sure it will be, those workers caught in the trap of management changes, unemployment, short-time work and having to move from one city to another, will have the right as federal employees covered by this legislation to bargain collectively with real power with their employers. I do not make this suggestion with any idea of stopping technological change or automation because, as I have indicated before, I do not know of a union which really believes it can stop technological change or, for that matter, one that really wants to do that. I make the suggestion because the workers have a right not to have to carry the whole burden resulting from the changes.
I do not suppose there is a city in Canada which has a higher percentage of railway workers than the city from which I come. There is not a member of parliament from the metropolitan Winnipeg area, whether an NDP, as three of us are, or a Liberal, as three other members are, who has not met people in Winnipeg who are railroad workers who have lived for 10 or 15 years in northern Ontario towns which were virtually wiped out as a result of the introduction of the diesel engine replacing the steam engine. No one questions the fact that the diesel engine is an improvement, is more efficient and economical and that the railways had to bring them forward, but what happened to the thousands of workers in these northern Ontario towns? Not only did they have to move from Kenora, Rainy River, Nakina and a host of other towns to Winnipeg, Thunder Bay or other major centres, as a result of these changes taking place, they lost their equity in their homes and they received virtually no recompense.
That is the kind of thing these people remember. That is the kind of thing the workers know about today and about which they are so concerned and upset. Unless we pass legislation to give them the right to deal fairly with their employers to blunt the brunt of this kind of dislocation, this is the kind of thing which will lead to illegal strikes, about which the public and members of parliament are equally concerned. I hope when this bill gets to the committee, where it will be discussed in detail clause by clause, the minister will make it clear that the doubts and fears I have expressed on the part of workers in Winnipeg and other cities will be allayed. I hope we will then have a bill giving that kind of protection to workers to which they are entitled in the 1970's.
